inline.s: Seeing Off the Reverend Xinglai as He Sets Out on Pilgrimage

The misty waters stretch, and stretch, and have no end;
A hundred folds of hill-towns lie behind.
All this to seek a teacher and ask the matter through —
Meghaśrī is not on Wondrous Peak to find.
Remembering the Thousand-Buddha Temple of the Great Capital

I recall that seven-jeweled terrace of a thousand flowers,
Where every bloom and leaf a Tathagata showed.
I wonder whether he, at leisure among the flowers,
Still thunders Dharma as in the days of old.
To the Chan Monk Nengzhe

Your road to Caoxi has not gone astray;
The pilgrimage before your eyes is not far away.
Think of the view when first you stepped past the gate:
Fragrant grasses everywhere — and where is home?
Sent to the Layman Wang

On a snowy night at Qingliang we talked of Chan;
Since we parted, twenty years have gone.
I often think of your true Vaiśālī face —
How many times has the cold moon grown round?
Again Passing Faxing Temple, Glad That Master Jiong Returns from Pilgrimage to Putuo

Three years have passed, and under the bodhi tree he has not sat;
One thought forever hangs the lamp of prajñā bright.
Do not say the dhūta monk does not preach the Dharma —
His bond with the Way is not a thicket-hunting monk’s.
Singing of the Lankavatara Room, Sent to the Laymen Tianyu and Kong

The surging sea of poison spreads without a shore;
Night yakṣas and rākṣasas make their home therein.
Only the Lankavatara’s priceless jewel
Shines day and night across the Ganges sands.

Eight-faced and luminous, its substance perfectly round;
Though vajra be keen, it cannot pierce it through.
Ever enshrined within the mind-king’s hall,
It shines through the three thousand and the great thousand worlds.
Caoxi Snow Tea, Sent to Master Zhen of Jinshan

I plucked one branch of leaf that comes before the spring
And send it to the crane-boned master in his illness.
Brew up a cup and taste it for yourself —
Is it as when you first called upon old Zhao?
In the Spring of the Jiachen Year, Ordered Back to the Garrison, My Boat Moored at the Zhijiang; Masters Yi and Jiong, Qinan, Yuzhong, and Zhongqian Came to Inquire, and So I Instructed Them

Awhile I moor my lone boat by the willow shade;
In quiet sitting it is like Jetavana’s grove.
Beneath the bodhi tree I ever keep the assembly —
No wonder you can come and ask the Dharma’s sound.
To Liang the Geomancer

Mountains, rivers, the great earth — one mote of dust;
Only a perfect, clear Dharma eye sees the truth.
Of course one must seek out the place where one belongs —
Would you consent to lie buried among the world’s idle folk?
To Yinzong, Abbot of Luofu Mountain

Beneath Luofu Mountain the Ganges circles round;
The grove beside it seems Putuo’s own ground.
If you would seek the Lord who watches within the flower,
Look at the bright moon falling into clear water.
To Zhou the Physiognomist

Drifting through rivers and lakes with a hempen-hilted sword,
Your wondrous art of reading hearts from Huqiu came.
Should a man ask you of flourishing and decline,
A band of true light lies within his two eyes.
To the Chan Monk Xingru Ji

Why journey south to imitate Sudhana’s road?
Seeking good friends, you long have wandered to and fro.
Upon the Wondrous Peak’s summit there is no trace —
Do not say Mañjuśrī pointed you there wrong.
To the Chan Monk Shenglin of Putuo

Below Putuo Mountain lies White Flower Village;
Day and night the tide’s voice preaches the Universal Gate.
Ask what the dweller of the hut can call his own —
Only parrots telling him the day is done.
Hearing That the Reverend Xinglai Has Received Full Ordination at Yunqi and Returned, I Send a Verse to Inquire After Him

One staff that lives and moves just like a dragon,
Your companion when you climbed Tianzhu’s crest.
Since at Yunqi you heard the Dharma taught,
Are all your karmic conditions laid to rest?
Summer Days in the Mountains

A bamboo bed, a tile for pillow, pine wind enough;
At noon I sleep so deep my dreaming thoughts run dry.
These four limbs and this hundred-boned frame are all but guests —
I do not know which one among them is the host.
The Bell in the Still of Night

The bell rings out through the cold sky of the clear night;
One stroke is like wind through ten thousand hollows blowing.
It does not idly urge the dragons to hear Dharma —
It comes to waken the true master, all unknowing.
To Mr. Zhou of Taihe

The great Way has always been before your eyes,
Yet you seek withered Chan where all is dead.
Who knows that every daily, ordinary thing
Is the supreme condition of the birthless ground?

How weak the power of the Way beside the power of karma!
Consider well which of the two is ripe, which raw.
If when you meet a state you can turn back and interchange,
At once the mad flight ends — Yajñadatta’s flaw.
To the Elder Zongchi of Yuantong

The West River’s stream flows down from Caoxi’s source;
Mazu’s headache — who has power to heal it?
If you would seek a living herb at Yuantong,
Ponder most of all the words: a dead cat’s head.
To Mr. Gong Boqi

A thousand li you traveled seeking one who knows,
Only to seek this mind from someone else’s hand.
But when you meet and see him face to face,
You learn how all your former searching was in vain.
To the Chan Monk Ciming Xian

With a single staff you came from far Duobao;
South you wandered, mist and water, one floating cup.
If on your homeward road you pass by Caoxi’s way,
The path is slick — do not tread the moss after rain.
Written at Random on Again Passing Through Yangcheng in the Summer of the Wushen Year

Thirteen years have passed since I crossed the immortal town;
In this human world I now have passed my sixtieth year.
Looking back on the dusty realm, it all is like a dream —
I do not know to what, in the end, it all belongs.

With one bowl I passed through every quarter then;
Each famous mountain served me as a place of practice.
I ate my fill of the benefactors’ rice, unpaid —
And still today the reckoning takes thought.

On Wutai, a thousand feet of snow buried my head;
I thought to be cold ash and, dying, be done.
Who would have guessed one single spark of fire
Would burn the whole great earth and sweep it in flood?

Once on the Eastern Sea I rode ten thousand li of waves;
Thunderous breakers shattered rock, the crests rode high.
Lightly on a single leaf I go with the wind,
Straight to tread the three isles and hook the six great turtles.
To the Attendant Zhengwei

At the very top of the hundred-foot pole on the cliff,
To shift a single step is hardest of all to do.
Just let go your hands and turn your body over —
And do not take it for a cat or a white ox.
To the Chan Monk Yue, Who Recites the Avatamsaka Sutra

A hundred cities, mist and water, seem like sky;
Where shall we meet to question Samantabhadra?
I think of you passing the Wondrous Peak’s summit —
I wonder whether he then told of this causation.
To the Rice Cook

When will Deshan come bearing his bowl?
Do not idly guess at his going to Changsha for rice.
Borrow nothing from the fragrance-kitchen above —
The matter by the stove is wondrous in itself.
Sent to Master Miaofeng of Wutai

A world of crystal, a palace of limpid glass;
Gold light and silver shine are everywhere the same.
Alone you stride astride a golden-haired lion —
Walking the eight directions, no wind can enter in.

Bones like frost and crane, your hair as silver-white;
Who knows you for Mañjuśrī’s final form?
Since in that cave we took our leave of one another,
Not even a mote of dust has come between.

My staff across my shoulder, I roam the sea of lands;
Boundless Buddha-fields are gathered in a single mote.
At leisure I split that mote of dust and look:
The phantom flowers have fallen, and but two eyes remain.

A thousand fathoms of cold cliff, a hundred feet of ice;
In those years we sat facing one another on the crags.
And now the burning house has turned a realm of cool —
One Vimalakīrti here, and here one monk.
Sent to Master Kongyin of Wutai

Afar I think of you at play in the flowered grove,
Sitting alone in shade of sandalwood and jeweled trees.
Your tongue’s root never stirs, and yet you preach the Dharma;
Ten thousand men now hear the sound of ocean tides.

Since I cast this body into the miasmic sea,
Barbarous smoke and poison mist have been my food.
Returning, I drink my fill of Caoxi’s water —
No less than Qingliang’s cold that pierces to the bone.
To the Master of the Purple Bamboo-Shoot Estate at Caoxi

One night of east wind fattened the purple bamboo shoots;
Boundless spring color reached my brushwood gate.
Peach blossoms fill the eye, and no one asks —
Who will present the upward turning, plain as day?
Sent to Zhiyin

Deep hidden at Baimen, at rest upon one branch;
Mountains and waters please the heart, world thoughts wear thin.
You once have entered Vimalakīrti’s little room —
A hundred thousand samādhis on a single hair’s tip.
To the Chan Monk Gao, in Seclusion

The six windows tightly closed, no wind can enter in;
For what matter do you hide your body here?
Just try the place where Mañjuśrī snapped his fingers —
It will press and crack the vast emptiness apart.
To the Chan Monk Rong, Abbot of the Zhongxiao Temple Built by Grand Marshal Guo of Taihe

Freed of the body, you came from the land of plague;
Three lives over, again you weave a magistrate’s tie.
In Vimalakīrti’s ten-foot room there is no word at all —
Do not say that wordlessness is not Chan.

The three mysteries of the upward way — each step a doubt;
The single phrase before all words — who may it know?
Unless you let your hands go at the cliff’s edge,
You throw away the two brows your mother gave.
Sent to Master Guifeng of Lingshan

The assembly on Vulture Peak still stands as then;
Pines and cypresses and cloud-dwellers fill the Deer Park.
It is the Dharma body that forever preaches —
Bell and drum clearly tell us that the dusk has come.
Sent to Master Jiewai of the Eastern Sea

Having yourself received the Vulture Peak’s entrustment,
Today you open the Dharma seat beside the sea.
The hosts of Māra on the Laṅkā summit —
How often have they come to hear you teach?
To the Chan Monk Nan

I ask about the ailing body there at Vaiśālī;
I do not know who it is that lies sick within.
Two times of gruel and rice, three times of medicine —
Eat them with clear knowing: that is closest to the truth.
Sent to the Layman Lai Guxuan

Long keeping fast, in one room you serve the King of Emptiness;
Within the mind-ground you ever burn the incense of prajñā.
Afar I think of your long days of cross-legged sitting,
Quietly hearing birdsong come out of the mountain light.
Sent in Thanks to the Layman Qinglian

I often think upon the layman Qinglian;
In dreams my soul keeps facing the man within the mirror.
I know you have deeply won the birthless meaning —
Sure that one may dwell in dust and not be stained.
Dwelling in the Dinghu Mountains

Having passed through every wind and wave of right and wrong,
This mind has long been used to forgetting all contrivance.
I turn about and go straight in among a thousand peaks,
Sitting to watch idle clouds fly through the bright day.
Sent to Master Mingzong

You once came from Tuṣita with the white gavel in hand;
Once the golden needle touched you, the Dharma eye opened.
Now will you spread the proclamation far and wide,
Only to leave the level ground swept clean of dust.
Sent to Master Yun

At the river’s head we sat knee to knee when we took leave;
Turning my head, green mountains enter my dreams.
I ask about the thousand hundreds on the flower terrace:
The single phrase before all words — how many know?
Sent to Master Chao

Wrapped in cloud and bearing the moon, full-fed on wind and frost;
Through the long clear night the crane’s dream stretches far.
You finish reading the Lankavatara, the incense spiral thins —
I know there is nothing left for you to ponder on.
Sent to Master Yu

Long have you appeared from Vulture Peak as the right vessel;
Who bothers to ask if clouds rise or flower rain falls?
Do not say the Dharma seat today is desolate —
In that cave you have become the multitude’s refuge.
To the Chan Monk Zhongfu Biao

Seeing through the ties of the world, you understood and returned;
A lotus in the midst of fire does not easily bloom.
Wash utterly clean the senses and their objects —
Do not let yourself enter that womb again.

Clear and bright, the Buddha-nature has no veil at all;
It was only one thought gone astray in times before.
You slipped and long sank down in the sea of birth and death —
This time, do not betray the lotus any more.
To the Chan Monk Weimi

Your bowl and bag have come from distant Funiu;
Crossing the ridge, the cold plum blossoms are opening.
If you would ask the intimate phrase of Caoxi:
Bodhi has no tree, and the mirror has no stand.
To the Chan Monk Ningzhi Han

With rounded crown and square robe, a body of eight treasures;
The first intent of leaving home is to transcend the dust.
If for the sake of afflictions you let yourself be lightly buried,
When next you raise your head the truth is already lost.
Sent to the Chan Monk Zhan, Dwelling on Funiu

You once took up a single bowl and came to Caoxi;
Would you refuse the road with only a thorn staff?
I hear that in the deep, hidden place of ten thousand hills,
The setting sun slants low and birds contend in song.
Sent to Inscribe the Rushi Cloister of Guo Cigong

At Shravasti the Jetavana grove was once laid out;
Now you would again take up the mind that spreads out gold.
Where the Dharma King thus fully raises it aloft,
Only Mañjuśrī is allowed to know the tune.
Reply to Guo Yunshu

You once came to Caoxi to ask about the supreme;
The secret meaning of the West belongs to Neng of the South.
Do not say that Vimalakīrti, who sealed his lips,
Was not the long-haired monk of former days.
Sent to Inscribe the Nangquan Pavilion at Taiyi, for Guo Shuzi

A clear pool, a bright moon, shadows deep and still;
Water in a pouch holds rivers and lakes, a heart of ferrying.
Ask where the swimming fish most truly flourish —
The Hao bridge is not necessarily the one who knows.
To the Chan Monk Hongfan

Having bowed in thanks before the thousand-flower jewel seat,
You then would seek the three mysteries from Linji.
And now you come to ask again the road to Caoxi —
Clouds fill the green hills, and the moon fills the sky.
Sent to Master Nayun

In broad daylight you split a single mote of dust;
Idly lifting your staff, its use is intimate.
Deep in the night of the bright moon, the tiger beneath the cliff
Takes refuge still as the man of former days.
Seeing Off the Monk Who Made a Sandalwood Image, Returning to Chaling

A branch of sandalwood from the Southern Sea;
The Dharma body shows its brows wherever it may be.
Welcomed home beneath the silent shade of pines,
It is as when the flower was held, and nothing said.
To Mr. Guo Lingxi

Long keeping fast, embroidering Buddhas, bowing to the King of Emptiness;
The burning house is turned into a ground for choosing Buddha.
At night you trim the bright lamp, the mind all still and quiet —
No need to think of lotuses away in the West.
Ten Poems Left in Farewell to the Brethren of the Lingnan Dharma Society, About to Depart for Nanyue

Once fallen into the world’s dust, twenty years have fled;
That we meet thus, you must believe, is karma from before.
Ever since the robe and bowl came to the south,
Today I take up once again the Chan of direct pointing.

The matter is plain and clear within your own person;
No need to ask outside about failure or success.
If only wherever you touch you turn the light around,
The toils of dust will never trap the master within.

The great Way from the first is beyond the true and false;
It is our discriminating that forces far and near.
You must see through the face your mother bore —
Then you are one set apart among the dusty world.

I have drunk the miasmic smoke to the dregs, and still my teeth are cold;
I do not remember now the hardness of the roads behind.
This time I go into the deep, secret place of ten thousand hills,
To watch the five-hued clouds and glow from where I sit.

Twenty years I galloped through the land of plague;
These years I never noticed my temples turn to frost.
Now I take a single leaf of boat and go —
My traces shall be hidden in ten thousand ravines.

Long have I mixed my traces in the dust and dimmed my light,
Only because I am busy raising up this matter.
The thousand-foot fishing pole is almost hewn away;
I turn to sea and sky, and all is vaster still.
